findings.summary: MSL is used in the TIME_WAIT explanation but never defined.

findings.summary: The ISN section's bullets are fragments that each hold a separate idea, and the second and third mix cause and effect without a clear label.

findings.fix: Rewrite as 'ISN random per connection → (1) stale packets from old connections rejected, (2) blind spoofing hard to guess', or use a two-row Benefit table.

findings.summary: Two ideas share the same page section: ISN and fast retransmit sit together under one heading, and the 'Interview Point' block is numbered as section 3 after a 'Remember' callout, so the structure is hard to skim.
findings.evidence: 2. ISN and Fast Retransmit ... 3. Interview Point
findings.fix: Split into 'ISN' and 'Fast Retransmit' sections, and keep the Interview Point block unnumbered like on other pages.

findings.summary: The cwnd bullet is placed before the formula and crams a definition and a cross-reference into one line, so the main rule is introduced after a tangent.

findings.summary: The section does not cover an outline point (missing "duplicate", "restarts").
findings.evidence: Timeout drops cwnd to 1 MSS and restarts slow start; 3 duplicate ACKs (Reno) halve cwnd and continue in fast recovery

findings.summary: MSS is used as the unit for cwnd and is never defined.
findings.evidence: "Slow start: cwnd ~10 MSS, doubles every RTT until ssthresh"; "cwnd = 1 MSS"
findings.fix: Define MSS (maximum segment size, the largest data payload per segment) on first use. Also define ssthresh and RTT, because the page 5 diagram and bullets use them without introduction.

findings.summary: The cwnd diagram's label shows 'doubling, then +1, then drop' while the bullets use ~10 MSS start and ssthresh is only marked at 41 after the loss, so a learner cannot tell which ssthresh ended slow start (the pre-loss threshold is never given).

findings.summary: The Loss Reaction section is written as arrow text lines rather than a table, and the repeated 'Loss signal?' prefix makes the comparison harder to scan.
findings.evidence: Loss signal? --timeout--> cwnd = 1 MSS, slow start

findings.summary: The cheat sheet's debug section shows a fix and an error explanation as a loose pair of lines, and the Quick recall block's handshake diagram is only labels with no ordering cue, mixing unrelated recall items.

findings.summary: The 'Mistakes to avoid' block is one run-on prose line of several items.
findings.evidence: Native VLAN mismatch. Assuming switches stop broadcasts. Expecting different VLANs to ping without routing. Trusting ARP replies blindly.
findings.fix: Turn it into a bulleted list, one mistake per bullet.

findings.summary: The cheat sheet lists 'ARP request is broadcast' under Frame and Switch Rules, then repeats it in the ARP section.
findings.evidence:
ARP request is broadcast
... Request is broadcast, reply is unicast
findings.fix: Remove the duplicate from the switch rules list.

findings.summary: The quiz answer for the first question skips the broadcast/unknown-unicast flooding step, so the reasoning is incomplete.
findings.evidence: "Only out port 1." / "A's first frame taught the switch A = port 1"
findings.fix: Add that C's frame is forwarded as known unicast to A because A's source MAC was learned from its first frame. Note that B's port 2 also saw A's first flooded frame, but C's frame is not sent there.

findings.summary: One bullet holds two ideas: the lookup rule and the MAC exclusion.
findings.evidence: Router looks up the destination IP, never the MAC
findings.fix: Split into 'Lookup key is the destination IP' and 'The MAC is never used for the route lookup'.

findings.summary: A bullet packs two ideas: the AD rule and the metric scope with its examples; the AD table is also followed by a prose-style worked example.
findings.evidence: RIP metric = hop count; OSPF metric = cost (from bandwidth)
findings.fix: Split into one bullet for the RIP metric and one for the OSPF metric, or put both in a small table (Protocol | Metric).

findings.summary: Code commands are shown before a one-line idea states what they do, and the Linux/Cisco labelling is left to a caption after the code.
findings.evidence:
bash
ip route add 10.2.0.0/16 via 192.168.1.1
ip route 10.2.0.0 255.255.0.0 192.168.1.1
Linux (first), Cisco (second)
findings.fix: State the idea first (e.g. 'Static route = destination prefix + next hop'), then show the two commands as separate labelled blocks, one for Linux and one for Cisco, and put the 'bash' language tag only on the Linux block.

findings.summary: The section does not cover an outline point (missing "independently", "identical").
findings.evidence: Link-state (OSPF, IS-IS): each router floods link states (LSAs) to all routers in the area, builds an identical map (LSDB), and runs Dijkstra's SPF independently to compute shortest paths
findings.fix: Add the point with an explanation and an example.

findings.summary: The BGP path-vector note is a prose paragraph holding three ideas, and it sits under the distance-vector pitfalls heading although it is not a pitfall.
findings.evidence: A third type: each prefix carries its full AS path. Seeing your own ASN means a loop, and policy can be applied.
findings.fix: Move it to its own section and make it three bullets: 'Each prefix carries its full AS path', 'Own ASN in the path = loop, reject', 'Policy can be applied on the path'.

findings.summary: The 'Max hop limit' bullet packs two facts, and the line reads awkwardly as 'RIP 15 is max'.
findings.evidence: Max hop limit: RIP 15 is max, 16 = unreachable
findings.fix: Split into 'RIP max is 15 hops' and '16 hops = unreachable (infinity)'.

findings.summary: The 'routing by rumour' phrase and 'Neighbours' word' are used loosely and the Config row says 'More design effort', mixing table terms, while page 5 uses 'Path-vector' as a protocol type with no link back.
findings.evidence: Config | Simple | More design effort
findings.fix: Add a Path-vector column or row to the comparison table, or reference the BGP page, so the three types are compared in one place.

findings.summary: The troubleshooting for a neighbour stuck at Init or ExStart drops the outline's timer and area mismatch causes, and the neighbour-state list gives no meaning for any state.
findings.evidence: "Init: one-way hellos (ACL, multicast). ExStart: MTU mismatch." The states appear only as bare names: "Down Init 2-Way ExStart Exchange Loading Full".
findings.fix: Add that hello/dead timer, area ID or authentication mismatches also stop neighbours from progressing. Give a one-line meaning for each key state, for example Init = hello seen but not yet bidirectional, 2-Way = bidirectional and DR election happens, Full = databases synchronised.

findings.summary: Several bullets hold more than one idea, and the OSPF neighbour-requirements line is a long run of items.
findings.evidence: Link-state IGP, IP protocol 89 / Multicast 224.0.0.5 all routers, 224.0.0.6 DR/BDR / Adjacency needs same area ID, hello/dead 10s/40s, subnet, authentication / Election is non-preemptive; DR cuts the number of adjacencies
findings.fix: Split each into single-idea bullets, e.g. 'IP protocol 89', '224.0.0.5 = all OSPF routers', '224.0.0.6 = DR/BDR', 'DR election is non-preemptive', 'DR reduces the number of adjacencies'; render the adjacency requirements as a checklist or table.

findings.summary: The Cisco config appears under 'Cisco Example' before the idea of the network statement and wildcard mask is stated; the explanation follows the code.
findings.evidence:
router ospf 1
 network 10.0.0.0 0.0.0.255 area 0
enable OSPF on matching interfaces
findings.fix: Put the one-line idea ('network + wildcard mask selects the interfaces that run OSPF in an area') above the code block, and note that 0.0.0.255 is a wildcard mask, not a subnet mask.

findings.summary: The best-path list gives no way to see that it is an ordered ranking, and uses terms without a one-line meaning; several bullets hold two ideas.
findings.evidence: Path-vector over TCP 179, neighbours set by hand / Own ASN already in AS_PATH → route rejected (loops)
findings.fix: Number the best-path steps 1–8 and split bullets so each holds one fact (transport, neighbours configured manually, loop check).

findings.summary: The BGP config is shown after the steps in prose and the verification bullet packs several ideas.
findings.evidence: Verify show ip bgp summary: number in State/PfxRcd ok; Idle/Active = TCP or config fault
findings.fix: Split into 'show ip bgp summary checks session state', 'A number in State/PfxRcd = session up', 'Idle/Active = TCP or config fault'.

findings.summary: The section does not cover an outline point (missing "administrative", "distance").
findings.evidence: Lookup order: longest prefix first, then lowest administrative distance, then lowest metric; 0.0.0.0/0 is the last resort
findings.fix: Add the point with an explanation and an example.

findings.summary: The Gotcha mixes two ideas, and 'Two DHCP servers on one LAN' is only a heading with no explicit cause or fix.
findings.evidence: "A rogue home router hands out conflicting gateways/DNS, so connectivity fails randomly."
findings.fix: Split into bullets: 'Cause: a second (rogue) DHCP server answers Discover first', 'Effect: wrong gateway/DNS', 'Fix: disable DHCP on the extra router or enable DHCP snooping'.

findings.summary: The trace is a flat list of fragments, and the Request step is described inconsistently across the page.
findings.evidence: "Client 0.0.0.0 sends Discover" / "Server 192.168.1.1 offers 192.168.1.50/24" / "gw 192.168.1.1, lease 24h"
findings.fix: Show the trace as a 4-row arrow diagram or table (client → server) with the offered IP, gateway and lease on the Offer row, and note that the Request is broadcast.

findings.summary: "Scope" and "pool" are central to the relay and setup comparison but are never defined for a learner meeting DHCP for the first time.
findings.evidence: "It stamps giaddr so the server picks the right scope"; "Remote subnet | Yes | one scope per subnet"; "Static IP | No | set on host, outside pool"
findings.fix: Add one line saying a scope is the pool of addresses the server hands out for one subnet, and that giaddr tells the server which subnet the request came from.

findings.summary: The relay config snippet is shown before the idea behind it is stated, and its explanatory line comes after the code.
findings.evidence: "It stamps giaddr so the server picks the right scope" / "interface Vlan20 ip helper-address 10.0.0.5" / "on the router interface facing the clients"
findings.fix: Put a one-line idea first, such as 'Point the client-facing interface at the DHCP server with ip helper-address', then show the code.

findings.summary: The setup table has a mislabeled header and a vague cell, and the lease timers are a vertical list where a timeline would read better.
findings.evidence: " | Relay? | Rule" and "Reservation | As for its subnet"
findings.fix: Name the first column 'Setup'. Change the reservation cell to 'Same as its subnet (relay if remote)'. Draw the lease timers as one timeline: Ack → T1 50% → T2 87.5% → Expiry.

findings.summary: "DF" is used on Page 3 but is never defined anywhere, and Page 5 uses it as if it were already known.
findings.evidence: Page 3: "4 = fragmentation needed and DF set"; Page 5: "DF bit | Packet bigger than MTU" (the DF bit is never expanded or explained as Don't Fragment).
findings.fix: On Page 3, define DF as the Don't Fragment flag in the IP header on first use. Or move the code 4 detail to Page 5 after DF is explained.

findings.summary: Type 3 codes and the type table are packed into one line, so a skimming learner can misread which number is the type and which is the code.
findings.evidence: "Type 3 codes: 0 net, 1 host, 3 port" / "4 = fragmentation needed and DF set"
findings.fix: Make a code sub-table: Code | Meaning (0 net unreachable, 1 host unreachable, 3 port unreachable, 4 fragmentation needed and DF set).

findings.summary: The commands are shown in a code block before the idea is stated, and the Linux traceroute final reply is labeled as 'Port Unreachable (3/3)' without explaining that the notation means type/code.
findings.evidence: "Port Unreachable (3/3)" and the code block "traceroute host     # Linux, UDP probes"
findings.fix: Add a one-line idea before the commands, and write 'Destination Unreachable, port (type 3 code 3)'. Keep the notation the same across pages.

findings.summary: The ping MTU test code appears right after the PMTUD diagram without a lead-in line stating its purpose, and the Gotcha bullets hold more than one idea.
findings.evidence: "ping -M do -s 1472 host   # Linux" / "Firewall blocks all ICMP: small requests work, large transfers hang."
findings.fix: Add 'Test the path MTU by pinging with DF set' before the code. Split the black-hole gotcha into cause (firewall blocks ICMP 3/4) and symptom (large transfers hang).

findings.summary: The cheat sheet's third section lists unrelated commands and fixes in one block, and it uses a trailing note line that is easy to misread as belonging to the wrong command.
findings.evidence: "ping -M do -s 1472 host  # 1472+28=1500" / "last line is the MTU test"
findings.fix: Put the '1472+28=1500, MTU test' comment inline on the command and drop the trailing line. Split 'Commands' and 'Troubleshooting order' into separate sections or a table.

findings.summary: The cheat sheet introduces the 169.254.x.x diagnostic, which no earlier page explains.
findings.evidence: "169.254.x.x address means DHCP failed"
findings.fix: Add a line on the DHCP page: 'No server answers, so the client self-assigns 169.254.x.x (APIPA)'. Keep the term the same on the cheat sheet.

findings.summary: Port-forwarding code is shown mid-page, and the 'Also needs a FORWARD allow and ip_forward=1' bullet holds two requirements.
findings.evidence: Also needs a FORWARD allow and ip_forward=1
findings.fix: Split into two bullets: 'Needs a FORWARD allow rule' and 'Needs net.ipv4.ip_forward=1'. Put the one-line idea before the code block.

findings.summary: The SNAT/DNAT flow is shown as a list of unconnected boxes, so it is unclear how the inbound DNAT path differs from outbound SNAT.
findings.evidence: Inside host / SNAT / NAT table / Reply (no DNAT flow shown)
findings.fix: Draw two labelled flows: outbound (host → SNAT → internet) and inbound (internet → DNAT → host), with the NAT table between them.

findings.summary: The 'Remember' callout restates the Mistakes bullet about the home-router DMZ host and adds a second idea (database inside).
findings.evidence: Router 'DMZ host' is not a real DMZ: no segmentation. The database stays inside.
findings.fix: Keep one idea in the callout, and leave the database point to the Mistakes list.

findings.summary: The IPsec vs TLS comparison table has a 'Needs' row whose TLS cell lists product names instead of a requirement, so the two columns do not compare the same thing.
findings.evidence: Needs | Client or hardware | OpenVPN, AnyConnect
findings.fix: Make the TLS cell a requirement, for example 'Needs | Client or hardware | Client, often a browser or app'. Put 'OpenVPN, AnyConnect' in a separate 'Examples' row.

findings.summary: The 'Needs' row in the IPsec vs TLS table is inconsistent and misaligned: the IPsec cell says 'Client or hardware' while the TLS cell lists products.
findings.evidence: Needs | Client or hardware | OpenVPN, AnyConnect
findings.fix: Make both cells the same kind of thing, e.g. IPsec: 'Gateway hardware or built-in OS client'; TLS: 'Client such as OpenVPN or AnyConnect'.

findings.summary: The 'Hosts' row in the VPN types table is ambiguous, and 'Split = less load, weaker control' holds two ideas.
findings.evidence: Hosts | Transparent, always on | Need a client
findings.fix: Rename the row to 'Client needed' with 'No' / 'Yes', and split the split-tunnel line into two bullets (less load; weaker control).

findings.summary: The WireGuard Mistakes section is a prose line that strings four problems together, and it is not formatted like the other pages.
findings.evidence: Overlapping AllowedIPs between peers, UDP port closed, wrong public key, no ip_forward on a gateway.
findings.fix: Make it a four-bullet list under a '3. Mistakes' style header.

findings.summary: The AllowedIPs bullet holds two ideas (routing and filtering) in a single line.
findings.evidence: AllowedIPs = outgoing routing table + incoming source filter
findings.fix: Split into 'Outgoing: picks the peer to send to' and 'Incoming: drops packets with sources outside the list'.

findings.summary: The debug order is a list of loose fragments in which each step and its action are separate lines, so the sequence is hard to follow. The commands are not mapped to the steps.
findings.evidence: Keys / proposals / Routes / AllowedIPs / Firewall / ports / MTU / clamp MSS
findings.fix: Use a numbered chain such as '1 Keys & proposals → 2 Routes & AllowedIPs → 3 Firewall ports → 4 MTU/MSS', and label each command with the step it checks.

findings.summary: The Check yourself page gives two answer lines per question with no indication of which is correct, and some of the lines are wrong or contradict each other.
findings.evidence: Only to B: the last configured peer takes the range, so A silently loses it. / A's packets with 10.0.0.x sources are dropped on arrival.
findings.fix: Give each question one clearly marked answer with a short reason. Fix the WireGuard answer: AllowedIPs overlap is a misconfiguration, and the result is not 'last peer wins' as stated.

findings.summary: The Mistakes section pairs a mistake with a fix by splitting them into stray lines, so the 'Make it HA' fix reads as a separate item.
findings.evidence:
One load balancer is not highly available
Make it HA
Run an active-passive or active-active pair behind a floating virtual IP.
findings.fix: Write the mistake and its fix as one 'Mistake -> Fix' pair, e.g. 'One LB is a single point of failure -> run an active-passive or active-active pair behind a floating virtual IP'.

findings.summary: The L4 and L7 bullets each hold several ideas, and L7 capabilities are repeated in prose and in the table.
findings.evidence: Also terminates TLS, rewrites headers, retries, compresses
findings.fix: Split into one-idea bullets or move the L7 extras into the comparison table as a 'Extras' row.

findings.summary: The 'Client IP is lost behind L7' mistake has a two-sentence explanation. It also names X-Forwarded-For and PROXY protocol together, which are two different fixes.
findings.evidence: Read X-Forwarded-For or enable PROXY protocol to get the real one.
findings.fix: List each as its own bullet: 'L7: read X-Forwarded-For' and 'L4/TCP: enable PROXY protocol'.

findings.summary: The sticky-sessions bullets mix two mechanisms with their downsides in one line.
findings.evidence:
Pin via cookie (L7) or source-IP hash (L4)
Skews balance; session lost if backend dies
findings.fix: Use one bullet per mechanism, and one bullet per downside.

findings.summary: The mistakes list packs two ideas into a bullet and the second mistake is ambiguous about the failure.
findings.evidence: Port-only check, or 200 while the database is down
findings.fix: Split into 'Port-only check' and 'Shallow check returns 200 while the DB is down'.

findings.summary: The cache-key bullets hold multiple ideas and the Vary/cookie guidance is unclear.
findings.evidence: Add Vary or cookies only if needed: each part lowers the hit ratio
findings.fix: Split into 'Cache key = host + path + query string' and 'Each extra key part (Vary, cookie) lowers the hit ratio, so add only when needed'.

findings.summary: Code is shown after the idea but the bullet states two ideas (versioned names and year-long max-age) in one line.
findings.evidence: Versioned names app.9f3a.js allow a year-long max-age with immutable
findings.fix: Separate into 'Version the filename' and 'Then set a year-long max-age with immutable'.

findings.summary: The nginx and HAProxy intro bullets each hold two ideas.
findings.evidence:
check runs the health probe; fall 3 down, rise 2 up
cookie SRV insert pins a client; cookie s1 names the server
findings.fix: Split each into one bullet per directive.

findings.summary: The 'Spoofable X-Forwarded-For' warning is a two-sentence prose block holding separate rules.
findings.evidence: Never use a client-sent value for access control or rate limits. Trust only what your own proxy appended; set the trusted proxy list explicitly.
findings.fix: Break into three bullets: never trust client-sent values, trust only your proxy's appended entry, set the trusted proxy list explicitly.

findings.summary: The algorithms-and-health list on the cheat sheet mixes algorithm picks with health and session rules under one heading, with no visual separation.
findings.evidence:
Round robin: uniform requests
Least connections: uneven or long requests
Consistent hash: cache or affinity needs
Probe a real /healthz, not just the port
Set fall/rise thresholds
findings.fix: Split into an algorithm table and a separate health-check checklist.

gaps: Physical layer basics: cabling, Wi-Fi/802.11, and wireless networking
Network performance concepts: bandwidth, latency, throughput
Network address translation details at the transport level are only covered inside ip-subnetting and network-security
Spanning Tree Protocol and link aggregation
Cryptography fundamentals (symmetric/asymmetric keys, hashing, certificates) needed for TLS and VPNs
Network monitoring and packet capture (Wireshark, tcpdump)
Email and other application protocols (SMTP, SSH, FTP)
overlaps: NAT is covered in both ip-subnetting and network-security
Layer-by-layer protocol and device roles in osi-tcpip repeat in later chapters
TTL appears in both dns (caching) and dhcp-icmp (hop limit)
TLS appears in both http-tls and network-security (TLS VPNs)
Hubs/switches/routers in osi-tcpip repeat in data-link-arp and routing-fundamentals
Broadcast and ARP concepts recur between data-link-arp and dhcp-icmp (DHCP discover)
Proxies, reverse proxies and DMZ/firewall placement recur between network-security and load-balancers-proxies-cdn
Anycast/BGP routing appears in both routing-fundamentals and load-balancers-proxies-cdn
